newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taipei invites HK over to mark Tiananmen post-97.
newsitem.headline: Taipei invites HK over to mark Tiananmen post-97.

text.p: Taipei on Thursday invited Hong Kong people to come to Taiwan to commemorate the 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in Beijing if such ceremonies are not allowed after China takes over on July 1.
Hong Kong activists have vowed they will not abandon annual gatherings to mark the anniversary of the military's crushing of the Tiananmen Square protests on June 4, 1989.
Some 55,000 people turned out for a candlelight vigil in Hong Kong on Wednesday night, driving the point home.

"After Hong Kong reverts to communist Chinese rule, it is unclear whether Hong Kong people are able to stage large-scale activities to commemorate the (pro-democracy) movement," Taiwan's state-run Central News Agency quoted Kao Koong-lian, vice chairman of Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council, as saying.
"If they are not allowed to do so in the future, the government welcomes Hong Kong people to hold such activities in Taiwan," Kao told a news conference.

Whether Hong Kong could maintain its democratic system and civil liberties after the colony was handed back to China at midnight on June 30, after 156 years of British rule, remained questionable, Kao said.
"We don't want such activity to be suspended," he added.

Taiwan leaders are suspicious of the so-called "one country, two systems" idea being pioneered in Hong Kong. China is trying out the model with an eye to Taiwan, which it would also like to bring back into the mainland fold.
Under the system agreed by Britain and China in 1984, Hong Kong can maintain its political and economic structures for 50 years after the handover.

Beijing, which has viewed Taiwan as a renegade province since the Nationalists fled there after losing a civil war in 1949, has said its handling of Hong Kong's return should reassure Taiwan about its own future with the mainland.
President Lee Teng-hui has rejected "one country, two systems" for Taiwan despite his government's official policy favouring eventual reunification with the mainland.

Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government, which has embraced multi-party democracy, maintains that reunification is impossible before the Communist Party drops its monopoly on power and allows political liberalisation.
